h: Written for the People Who Specify and Approve
t: 3.0 Audience Design Architects and designers You are choosing the stone, the panel sizes and the joint pattern, and need to know which fixing system and thickness make them buildable. Review Consultants and facade engineers You write or review the specification and the submittals, and want to see the process, the tests and the records before the work starts. Delivery Main contractors' technical offices You prepare prequalification and submittal packages and need a stone subcontractor whose statements hold up when the consultant reads them. AL-Swati Contracting is based in Riyadh. Our team's experience goes back to 1994. Our scope is the supply and installation of mechanically fixed natural stone (mainly Riyadh limestone), marble, granite and porcelain facades, and the installation of the steel substructure behind them to the engineer's design.

h: What We Install, Scope and Limits
t: 4.0 Scope What we install Systems: Up-Down angles, pin (PEN) fixing, C-Channel , kerf rail and undercut anchors. Undercut experience: Hilti undercut anchors on 30 mm natural stone and on 20 mm porcelain, on an ongoing commercial project for a major Saudi main contractor. Brackets and angles: stainless steel or hot-dip galvanised steel, according to the project specification. Anchor and bolt sizes: per the engineer's calculation and the consultant's specification. Thickness: natural stone typically 30 mm, thicker on demand; marble and granite often 20 mm. Exterior 20 mm panels on edge fixings need the engineer's check and stone tests, or an undercut system. Brands we can install: Hilti, fischer, Rockany, and local or imported accessories. Warranty: a 5-year written workmanship warranty attested by the Chamber of Commerce, issued by the contracting company. Scope and limits Design is by the project engineer or consultant: we install to approved shop drawings, issued to us or prepared by the project's facade engineer. Brand names say what we can install; we hold no manufacturer certification. Sizes, wind values and stone strengths belong to each project's calculation and tests.

1.0 Scope We supply and install mechanically fixed natural stone (mainly Riyadh limestone), marble, granite and porcelain facades. We also install the steel substructure behind them, to the engineer's design. Installation is by our own team with a site supervisor. The fixing systems we install are Up-Down angles, pin (PEN) fixing, C-Channel , kerf rail and undercut anchors. They are compared on the fixing systems page.

2.0 Engineering Route A We install to your approved shop drawings The consultant or the main contractor supplies approved shop drawings. We install to them and raise any site conflict before proceeding. Route B Engineering within our scope The project's facade engineer prepares the design basis, wind loads per the current SBC 301, calculations for the steel substructure, shop drawings and a part list, and visits the site weekly. On both routes the design belongs to the project engineer or consultant, and the installation follows the approved documents. Under the Law of Practising Engineering Professions (Art. 8), accredited engineers write their name, professional grade and accreditation number on their engineering works [1] . Wind loads are calculated for each project to the current SBC 301 [2] ; the calculation states the code edition used.

3.0 Step by step Enquiry and drawings We review the elevations, the stone, the backup wall and the heights, and say which fixing systems suit them. You can start with the send drawings form. Engineering route agreed Route A (your approved shop drawings) or Route B (shop drawings and calculations by the project's facade engineer, within our scope) is fixed before pricing is final. Material submittals and samples Stone samples that show the range, and data for the fixings, brackets and anchors, are submitted for approval. Bracket material is stainless steel or hot-dip galvanised steel, according to the project specification. Mock-up On request Built from the approved materials and drawings, by the same crew, and kept as the benchmark once approved. Setting out Grid and level lines are set and the wall is checked against the drawings before any anchor is drilled. Steel substructure Wall brackets, channels or frames are installed to the engineer's design. Anchor and bolt sizes are per the engineer's calculation and the consultant's specification. Anchor pull-out tests On request Arranged with the anchor manufacturer or a testing laboratory, and witnessed by the consultant. Stone installation By our own team with a site supervisor, panel by panel to the approved drawings: fixing engagement, clearances and joints are checked as the work rises. Engineer's site visits Route B On Route B projects the facade engineer visits the site weekly. Handover Final inspection and snagging with the consultant, the project records, and the maintenance and handover guide . Warranty A 5-year written workmanship warranty attested by the Chamber of Commerce, issued by the contracting company.

4.0 Behind the stone We install the steel substructure; the engineer designs it. These are the points a design basis for a substructure normally settles, with the published guidance behind them. They are general guidance, not project values. Wind. Wind loads on the stone and its supports are calculated for each project to the current SBC 301, and the design pressures are stated on the documents [2] . Stiffness. Stone tolerates very little movement of its support. ASTM C1242 treats a backup more flexible than L/600 as a case for a stone specialist [3] ; the limit used is the engineer's decision. Anchors to concrete. The steel of the bolt is only one check. A steel connection program does not prove the concrete side: pull-out, bond and splitting come from the anchor's own technical data [4] . A separate anchor calculation for the actual product is part of the design. Hollow block. Anchors in hollow masonry have low capacity in the maker's published data [5] , and one maker states it has no test data for the top of an ungrouted hollow wall [6] . Loadbearing brackets and frames go to reinforced concrete unless the engineer proves otherwise by tests. Corrosion protection. Hot-dip galvanising is specified to a standard with a minimum coating thickness [7] ; hollow sections need vent and drain holes [8] ; site cuts and welds remove the zinc and are repaired by a named method [9] . Dissimilar metals. Stainless fasteners on larger galvanised or carbon steel parts cause little problem; the reverse arrangement is the dangerous one. Where the joint can stay damp, the metals are separated with isolating washers or pads [10] [11] . Movement. Steel moves roughly two to two and a half times as much as stone with temperature [12] . Each member has a fixed point and sliding points, and the stone has movement joints where the engineer places them. Tolerances. Structural steel tolerances are looser than stone tolerances [13] , so the adjustment range is designed into the bracket between frame and stone. Reference drawings Load path on vertical channels Steel substructure Typical details for discussion at design stage, not for construction. Notes on these details

5.0 Your side Architectural elevations and wall sections (PDF or DWG), with building height and storey heights. The stone or panel: type, finish, panel sizes and the thickness you have in mind. The backup wall: reinforced concrete, solid block, hollow block or a mix. The project specification section for stone cladding, if one exists. If not, our guide specification is a starting point. Which engineering route you prefer, A or B.

1.0 One table System Mechanism Best use Typical panel thickness (published guidance) Concealed or visible Replacing one panel Limits What we have done Up-Down angle One angle with a split tongue: one half turns up into the panel above, the other down into the panel below [1] . Low and medium rise, regular coursing, solid backup, stone of 30 mm and more. 30 mm practical minimum, as for all edge fixings [2] ; about 32 mm general minimum in US guidance [3] . Concealed in the joint. Difficult: one bracket holds two panels. The industry guide prefers individual anchors [1] . Edge slots weaken thin panels. The tongue must not rest on the panel below. One of the systems our team installs. Pin (PEN / dowel) A bracket carries a round pin that enters holes drilled in the edges of two adjacent panels. Bottom pins carry weight; top pins restrain against wind. The most common hand-set system for stone of 30 mm and more on concrete or solid masonry. 30 mm for pin-fixed panels in the German rule read here (older edition) [2] ; about 32 mm in US guidance [3] . Concealed in the joint. Panels are fixed in sequence, so a single panel is hard to release. Needs enough stone on each side of the hole [2] [4] ; a sliding sleeve on one side; break-out strength proven by test, never by epoxy [5] . One of the systems our team installs. C-Channel Vertical steel channels on wall brackets and anchors. The stone brackets (pin, Up-Down or kerf clips) bolt to the channel. Hollow block or weak infill walls, large cavities, tall storeys: the channels span to the concrete. Set by the stone fixing used on the channel. Concealed behind the stone. As for the stone fixing used. Channels, brackets and anchors need calculation; fixed and sliding points per channel; site cuts in galvanised channels need coating repair [6] . One of the systems our team installs. Kerf rail The blade of a rail or clip sits in a sawn slot (kerf) along the top and bottom edges of the panel, locally or continuously [7] . Regular grids of equal panels and rail-based ventilated facades. At least 10 mm of stone on each side of the groove in the German rule [2] ; in practice 30 mm and more. Concealed in the joint. Limited: a broken local kerf cannot be repaired, the panel is replaced [1] . Kerfs are cut in the workshop, not by hand grinder. No rigid epoxy fill: it has spalled stone through thermal expansion [8] . Kerf damage can hide on the back face [9] . One of the systems our team installs. Undercut anchor A hole with a widened base is drilled in the back of the panel; the anchor locks into it by shape. A hanger on the anchor hooks onto a horizontal rail [10] [11] . Thin hard stone, large panels, soffits and reveals, open-joint ventilated facades. From 20 mm for granite-type stone; 25 to 30 mm for limestone and sandstone in one maker's data [10] . Stoneware panels from 8 mm in one anchor's assessment [12] . Fully concealed: nothing in the joints. Each panel hangs alone and can be replaced. Holes are drilled with the maker's machine and checked with its gauge. Stone not listed in the anchor's assessment needs tests [10] . Higher cost. Hilti undercut anchors on 30 mm natural stone and on 20 mm porcelain, on an ongoing commercial project for a major Saudi main contractor. Porcelain clip or edge groove Stainless clips hold the panel edges on vertical profiles: visible clips, or concealed clips in a milled edge groove [13] [14] . Porcelain and ceramic slabs on a ventilated substructure. By the slab maker's system: clips for thin meshed slabs; a concealed edge groove needs a 20 mm slab; undercut and kerf need 12 or 20 mm slabs in one maker's guide [13] [14] . Visible (clips) or concealed (edge groove). Depends on the maker's system. The panel maker's rules apply, not stone rules. No site-cut kerfs in thin slabs. Mesh backing keeps fragments in place if a panel breaks; it is not a fixing [13] [15] . Porcelain facades are in our scope. Our undercut experience on 20 mm porcelain is noted above. 2.0 Choosing The backup wall. Reinforced concrete takes brackets directly. Hollow block usually means channels or frames spanning to the concrete. The panel thickness. Edge fixings ( Up-Down , pin, kerf) need about 30 mm of stone. Thinner hard stone and porcelain point to undercut anchors or the panel maker's own system. See thickness and fixing . Replaceability. If single panels must be removable for maintenance, each panel needs its own fixings: undercut on rails does this. The joints. Open-joint ventilated facades suit rail systems; sealed joints suit hand-set fixings. Evidence required. For natural stone, the assessed fixings we found in published sources are undercut anchors [16] [17] ; some porcelain panel systems hold their own assessments [13] .

3.0 Materials and brands Brackets and angles are stainless steel or hot-dip galvanised steel, according to the project specification. Anchor and bolt sizes are per the engineer's calculation and the consultant's specification; we do not publish sizes. As general guidance, published sources recommend stainless steel for the parts in direct contact with the stone, such as pins, tongues and kerf blades [4] [1] [3] . One of them accepts hot-dip galvanised parts only where they do not touch the stone [1] . The project specification decides. We can install systems from Hilti, fischer and Rockany [18] , and local or imported accessories.

1.0 Load path Open the drawing Detail 01 · Section Load path on vertical channels Principle The dead load and the wind load of every panel must reach the reinforced concrete structure: slab edges, beams or columns. Infill walls Hollow block and other infill walls are not counted on to carry the cladding. Where the wall behind the stone is infill, the brackets go to the concrete and vertical channels span between them. Fixed and sliding points Each vertical member has one fixed point that carries its weight, and sliding points that hold it against wind and let it move with temperature. The engineer places them. Who decides The load path, the member sizes and spacing and the anchors are the project engineer's design. See how we deliver .

2.0 Sections One vertical section per system, drawn the same way so they can be compared: wall on the left, stone on the right, numbered parts and a legend. The systems are compared in words on the fixing systems page. Open the drawing Detail 02 · Section Up-Down angle fixing How it carries The upper panel bears on the blade of the angle and its bottom kerf sits on the up-tongue. The down-tongue restrains the top of the panel below; a clear gap under the blade keeps weight off that panel. Typical use Low and medium rise, regular coursing, solid backup wall, stone of 30 mm and more. Check before approval Kerf width and depth and the stone left on each side of it; the slotted hole for level adjustment; bracket material per the specification; anchor type per the engineer's calculation. Open the drawing Detail 03 · Section PEN (pin) fixing How it carries A bracket carries a pin that enters holes drilled in the edges of two adjacent panels. Bottom pins carry weight; top pins restrain against wind. Typical use Hand-set stone of 30 mm and more on concrete or solid masonry. Check before approval Stone on each side of the hole; a sliding sleeve on one side of the pin; the break-out strength at the hole proven by test in the project stone. Open the drawing Detail 04 · Section Vertical C-Channel How it carries Wall brackets anchored into slab edges or beams carry vertical steel channels. The stone brackets bolt to the channels, so the infill wall carries nothing. Typical use Hollow block or weak infill walls, large cavities and tall storeys. Check before approval Calculation of channels, brackets and anchors; one fixed point and sliding points per channel; coating repair at site cuts in galvanised channels; separation of dissimilar metals. Open the drawing Open the drawing Detail 05 · Section and elevation Kerf rail system How it carries The blade of a horizontal rail sits in a kerf sawn along the top and bottom edges of the panels. The rail is continuous along the row and is fixed to the wall or to vertical profiles. Typical use Regular grids of equal panels and rail-based ventilated facades; stone of 30 mm and more. Check before approval Kerfs cut in the workshop, not by hand grinder; no rigid epoxy fill in the kerf; rail fixing spacing per the engineer; rail joints and movement. Open the drawing Open the drawing Detail 06 · Section and elevation Undercut anchors on rails How it carries An anchor locks by shape into an undercut hole in the back of the panel. A hanger on the anchor hooks over a horizontal aluminium rail, and the rails are screwed to vertical profiles fixed to the structure. Each panel hangs on its own and the face stays whole. Typical use Thin hard stone, porcelain, large panels, and facades where single panels must be replaceable. Check before approval The anchor's assessment covers the stone, or tests are done; holes drilled with the maker's machine and checked with its gauge; number and position of anchors per the assessment and the engineer. Our experience Hilti undercut anchors on 30 mm natural stone and on 20 mm porcelain. The drawings show the arrangement as we build it: wall brackets, vertical profiles, horizontal rails, then the panels.

3.0 Behind the stone Open the drawing Detail 07 · Elevation Steel substructure What it is Vertical steel members fixed to the columns, beams or slab edges. Where the fixing system needs them, horizontal rails are added. We install it; the engineer designs it. Why it is used It takes the cladding load past infill walls, spans tall storeys and gives a true plane to set the stone from. Check before approval Design basis and wind loads per the current SBC 301; deflection limit of the members; corrosion protection; fixed and sliding points; the adjustment range between structure and stone.

h: How Far the Stone Stands Off the Wall
t: 4.0 Stand-off Walls are never perfectly plumb, and a design may want the stone face a certain distance out. How that distance is made up decides the fixing, in three steps: Stand-off wanted Solution How the line is brought true Note Small, on a sound wall Up-Down angles (or pin brackets) fixed straight to the wall. By the size of the angle. Common sizes on Riyadh sites are 40 × 40, 40 × 50 and 40 × 60 mm, 3 mm thick; the longer leg sets the stone further out. A longer angle bends more and pulls harder on its anchor, so the engineer checks the angle and the anchor for the stand-off chosen. Moderate, or an uneven or weak wall Vertical C-Channel on wall brackets. Common channel: 41 × 41 mm, 2 or 3 mm thick, in 3 m lengths. By wall brackets of different lengths, which take up the wall's deviations, and by their slotted holes. The brackets go to the concrete. Channel size and bracket spacing are the engineer's. Large: deep cavities, projecting features A steel frame designed for the project, fixed to columns, beams or slab edges. The frame itself is set out to the stone line. Any of the fixing systems can then be mounted on the frame. Undercut and kerf rail systems Rails on vertical profiles or on the frame. The profiles or the frame are set out to line; the hanger or the rail does not change size. The hanger's screw sets the last few millimetres of level. As built on our undercut work. The engineer chooses the vertical members from the panel weight (dead load), the wind load on their span and the deflection the stone can accept. Sizes named here are the common ones on site, for orientation only; the project sizes are on the approved shop drawings.

h: Channel or Frame, and the System on It
t: 5.0 Choosing Many specifications require the cladding load to go to the reinforced concrete and not to the block wall. Two substructures do that, and the choice between them is mostly a question of span: Where the concrete is Substructure Why Close together: beams, columns, lintels and slab edges within short distances Vertical C-Channel on wall brackets anchored in the concrete. The channel only has to span from bracket to bracket across the block. Only at each floor: a full storey of block between slab edges A heavier section or a steel frame designed for the project. Over a storey-high span a light channel can deflect too much under wind. The engineer sizes the member for that span. Stone set far out from the wall A steel frame. See the stand-off table above. The fixing system is then chosen for the stone and the look. Each has its strengths and its limits: System Strengths Limits Up-Down and PEN Economical and quick; known to every stone fixer; easy to adjust panel by panel. A kerf or a hole is cut in the panel edge, so the stone needs thickness there: typically 30 mm. Kerf rail The continuous rail brings the row to line by itself; fast on large regular surfaces. The kerf runs along the whole edge, so the stone must be sound and the kerf cut in the workshop. Undercut anchors Nothing shows; no load on the panel edges; large panels; a single panel can be taken off and replaced. The highest cost; the holes need the maker's drilling machine and trained fixers.

6.0 On site Our usual practice on Riyadh sites. The approved shop drawings and method statement govern on each project. Item Our practice Up-Down and PEN: fixings per panel Each panel is held at four points: two fixings at its top edge, one towards each end, and the two fixings of the course below at its bottom edge. Every angle or pin therefore serves two courses. Larger panels get more, per the shop drawings. C-Channel : channel positions Channels are set out from the panel size, so that two brackets fall behind every panel. Steel frame Verticals first, then horizontals at the levels the panel size requires. Kerf rail Rails at the top and bottom edges of the panels; at the sides as well where the design calls for it. Undercut anchors Four hangers on the back of a panel on our current work (panels of 410 × 700 mm). The number per panel comes from the anchor's assessment and the engineer. Joints Open joints of 3 mm or 5 mm, kept uniform with cross-shaped spacers at the panel corners. Pin holes and kerfs Filled at the fixing with a two-part stone adhesive (resin and hardener). The product is submitted for approval with the materials. Anchors Into concrete or solid masonry. In hollow block only as the engineer and the anchor maker's instructions allow. Anchors are Hilti, Fischer or an approved equal that meets the project's requirements; holes are cleaned as the maker instructs. First course Set on a starter angle at the base, levelled before any stone goes up. Reveals, sills and copings Held by the same mechanical means: brackets from the channel, or a kerf in the piece. Movement joints Where the engineer shows them on the drawings. Pull-out tests on anchors Carried out by the consultant or the main contractor. If they are required from us, they are priced as a separate item. Waterproofing and insulation behind the stone Installed by us when they are in our scope: bituminous waterproofing on the wall, and insulation where specified.

7.0 Corners Open the drawing Detail 08 · Plan Four ways to turn a corner A · Butt joint One panel runs past the corner and the other stops against it. The edge of the first panel shows on the return face, so that edge is finished like the face. Simple and robust. B · Mitre Both panels are cut at 45° and meet on the corner line. The cleanest look, with the sharpest and most fragile edge: better above street level than beside a pavement. C · Quirk mitre A mitre with a small flat nose left on each panel. The edge is no longer a knife edge, so it takes knocks better. The usual choice for a crisp corner. D · Solid corner piece An L-shaped piece cut from a thicker block turns the corner in one stone, with no joint on the corner line. It costs more stone and more cutting. How a clean corner is made The corner pieces are cut in the workshop on a bridge saw or CNC machine, as a pair from the shop drawings, not by hand grinder on site. The sharp edges are eased slightly, and the pair is dry-fitted before fixing. Fixing and joint Each leg of the corner is carried by its own fixings; adhesive in a mitre is not the fixing. A joint is kept at the corner so the two faces can move with temperature. Decide early The corner type is shown on the shop drawings and built into the mock-up, together with window reveals, sills and copings.

h: What the Two Assessed Anchors Have in Common
t: 2.0 Undercut anchors The hole. Drilled in the back of the panel with the maker's machine, cylindrical first and then widened at the base; every hole is checked with the maker's gauge [1] [5] . The layout. Hilti's data gives four anchors per panel in a rectangular layout, a largest panel of 3.0 m² and minimum edge distances [1] . The engineer sets the positions from the assessment. The stone. Each assessment covers selected natural stones. A stone that is not listed needs tests to the assessment document before it is used [1] . The rail. A hanger on each anchor hooks over a horizontal rail, so each panel hangs on its own. The rails and brackets are part of the system design. The section and the back-of-panel view are on the typical details page. Porcelain. Thin ceramic and stoneware panels use their own anchors and assessments, tied to the panel maker's system [14] [15] . Reference drawings Undercut anchors on rails Undercut anchors: back of the panel Typical details for discussion at design stage, not for construction. Notes on these details

h: What an ETA Covers and What It Does Not
t: 3.0 An assessment An ETA describes the anchor: its materials, the hole, the resistance in the stones that were tested, and the assumptions of use [3] [7] . It does not approve a facade. The panel size, the wind load, the rail, the brackets and the anchors to the structure are the project engineer's calculation. It does not cover every stone. Riyadh limestone is a trade name for stone from several quarries, so the actual source is tested unless the maker confirms it in writing. It is not a certificate held by the installer. We can install these systems; we hold no manufacturer certification.

h: What to Ask the Maker For
t: 4.0 For a project The current assessment with its annexes and the declaration of performance. Written confirmation that the project stone is covered, or the test plan if it is not. The system proposal: rails, brackets and anchors, with the static calculation for the project's wind loads. The drilling machine, the gauge and operator training. Site pull-out tests and site support, where the specification asks for them. For Rockany systems: the datasheet with the aluminium alloy and the stainless grade, and the project calculation. In the guide specification , a maker's engineered system is Option B and assessed undercut anchors are Option C. Our experience with undercut fixing is with Hilti anchors, on 30 mm natural stone and on 20 mm porcelain. Hilti, fischer and Rockany are names of their owners. They are named here to say what we can install and where the published data comes from.

1.0 One table Material What it is Typical thickness we install Material standard Check before approval Riyadh limestone (beige and yellow) Local limestone, the facade stone of Riyadh. A trade name: it comes from several quarries and beds. Typically 30 mm, thicker on demand. ASTM C568 classifies limestone in three classes by density [1] . Tests on the actual quarry source; range samples that show the colour variation. White Riyadh stone The light, near-white local limestone. Typically 30 mm, thicker on demand. ASTM C568, as above [1] . As above. Light stone shows stains most clearly; mechanical fixing leaves no mortar behind the stone. Travertine A banded stone with natural voids, filled or unfilled. Sold as travertine marble. Typically 30 mm. ASTM C1527 covers travertine [2] . Direction of the bedding in the panel; filled or unfilled finish; tests at the project thickness. Marble Crystalline stone that takes a polish. Mostly imported. Often 20 mm. Exterior 20 mm panels on edge fixings need the engineer's check and stone tests, or an undercut system. ASTM C503: absorption 0.20% at most, flexural strength 6.9 MPa at least, soundness Group A for exterior use [3] . The soundness group; behaviour in heat (see below); test reports for the named marble. Granite Hard, dense igneous stone. Often 20 mm, with the same condition as marble. ASTM C615 covers granite [2] . Test reports for the named granite; the fixing type for 20 mm panels. Sandstone and other natural stone Quartz-based stone, basalt and other stones a project may call for. We install them on the same basis: the fixing follows the tested strength. Typically 30 mm. ASTM C616 covers quartz-based stone [2] . Tests on the actual source; bedding direction in the panel. Large-format porcelain Manufactured slabs, uniform in colour. By the slab maker's system. ISO/TS 17870-3 covers its mechanical fixing [4] . The slab maker's facade guide and the anchor's assessment for that slab. Why thickness follows the fixing, and what 20 mm panels need, is explained on the thickness and fixing page.

Glossy and reflective; the deepest colour. Marble, granite, dense limestone. Outdoors, polished marble loses gloss with weather. Shows scratches most. Honed Ground smooth and stopped before the gloss. Flat and matte. All stones. The usual finish for limestone facades. Sawn Left as the saw cut it. Matte, with faint saw lines. Limestone, sandstone, travertine. The most economical finish. Brushed (leathered) Worked with abrasive brushes that follow the grain. Soft satin, slightly uneven. Limestone, marble, granite. Hides small marks better than honed. Sandblasted Blasted with a fine abrasive. Even, fine roughness. Limestone, sandstone, granite. Rough finishes hold more dust than smooth ones. Bush-hammered Struck with a hammer that has many points. Evenly pitted. Limestone, granite, sandstone. A percussion finish needs a slab of at least 30 mm to be applied [5] . Flamed The surface is burst with a flame. Rough and crystalline. Granite. It removes material from the face: agree the thickness with the fabricator. Split-face Split, not sawn. A rough natural break. Limestone, sandstone. Thicker and heavier pieces; the engineer sizes the fixing for them. h: Riyadh Limestone Is a Trade Name
t: 5.0 Local stone There is no single data sheet for Riyadh limestone. Published figures for Riyadh carbonate rock differ widely: one academic study of hard limestone in Riyadh reports water absorption around 9% [8] , while trade sources quote much lower values. That range runs across the classes of ASTM C568, which allow at most 12%, 7.5% and 3% absorption for low, medium and high density limestone [1] . So the class and the design strength of a facade's limestone come from current tests on the quarry source that will supply the project. This is why we publish no strength value, and why range samples and test reports are part of the material submittal.

6.0 Imported stone Marble in the sun. Thin marble outdoors can bow and lose strength under repeated heating [9] . A European test exists for it (EN 16306) [10] . For exterior marble in Riyadh, ask the engineer whether it is required. Soundness. ASTM C503 limits exterior marble to soundness Group A [3] . Veined and decorative marbles in other groups belong indoors or need the engineer's review. Granite. Dense and strong. The fixing type still decides whether a 20 mm exterior panel is acceptable. Supply. Most marble used in Saudi Arabia is imported [11] . Each imported stone needs the quarry's current test reports, and a petrographic check where the stone is unfamiliar [12] .

7.0 Submittal Range samples. Several samples that show the lightest, the darkest and the most veined stone that will be accepted, in the project finish. Test reports. Absorption and density, compressive strength, flexural strength and the strength at the fixing. The list with ASTM and EN numbers is in the tests table . Finish and thickness. Bending tests are done at the project thickness and finish, because some finishes remove thickness [6] [7] . No substitution. Once approved, the stone source stays as approved unless the consultant approves a change in writing. See quality .

1.0 Short answer Natural stone, mainly Riyadh limestone: typically 30 mm, thicker on demand. Marble and granite: often 20 mm. Exterior 20 mm panels on edge fixings ( Up-Down , pin, kerf) need the engineer's check and stone tests, or an undercut system. Porcelain: the thickness and the fixing come from the panel maker's system. Wind loads are calculated for each project to the current SBC 301 [1] , and the stone values come from tests on the actual stone. Nothing on this page replaces that calculation.

h: Why 30 mm for Pin, Kerf and Up-Down
t: 2.0 Edge fixings An edge fixing sits in a hole or slot cut into the panel edge. What holds the panel is the stone left on each side of that hole. Published rules set a minimum for it: The German rule read here (an older edition of DIN 18516-3) asks for at least 10 mm of stone on each side of a pin hole or groove, and 30 mm minimum thickness for pin-fixed panels [2] . BS 8298-2, as reported by a stone engineer, asks for 12 mm on each side of a fixing mortice in strong stone and 25 mm in weaker stone, unless testing proves otherwise [3] . US industry guidance puts mechanically attached exterior panels at about 32 mm (1¼ in) as a general minimum [4] . Add the hole to 10 mm of stone on each side and the result is 28 to 30 mm. That is why 30 mm is the practical floor for edge fixings, and why a 20 mm panel cannot meet these geometry rules. Reference drawings Up-Down angle fixing PEN (pin) fixing Kerf rail system Typical details for discussion at design stage, not for construction. Notes on these details

3.0 Bending Wind bends the panel between its fixings. For a strip of panel spanning a distance L between two lines of support under a pressure w, textbook beam theory gives the bending stress as: stress = 0.75 × w × L² ÷ t² The thickness t is squared. With the same panel and the same wind: Change in thickness Bending stress becomes 30 mm to 25 mm 1.44 times higher 30 mm to 20 mm 2.25 times higher This is a simplification for explanation. Real panels on four point fixings are analysed as plates, and the stone around each fixing is checked separately [5] [6] . If either check fails, the answer is thicker stone, a smaller panel, more fixings or a different fixing type. The same panel in the same wind ⁦30 mm⁩ ⁦1.00 ×⁩ ⁦25 mm⁩ ⁦1.44 ×⁩ ⁦20 mm⁩ ⁦2.25 ×⁩ Bending stress, with 30 mm taken as 1. A simplification for explanation: real panels are analysed as plates.

4.0 Safety factors Stone varies from block to block, so the factors applied to its tested strength are large. Published values run from 3 to 8 and above, depending on the stone and the document: Source Factor on tested strength Note ASTM C1242 table (2016 edition preview) [7] Granite 3; marble (soundness Group A) 5; limestone 6; sandstone 6; travertine 8 Generally accepted values; the engineer may adjust them Natural Stone Institute, limestone chapter [8] 8 for wind or seismic loads; 10 for concentrated loads Limestone BS 8298 as reported in 2009 [5] Between 3 and 6, depending on the part and on whether mean or lowest expected values are used To be checked against the current edition DIN 18516-3, older edition [2] 3 on a statistical lower-bound value from at least 10 tests Pin fixing and bending Undercut anchor maker's design method [9] Partial factor 1.8 on stone resistance Limit-state format; not comparable one to one with the rows above The factor used on a project is the engineer's decision under the code named in the specification. Wet strength can be lower than dry strength, and some finishes remove thickness [5] [8] .

h: What 20 mm Marble or Granite Needs
t: 5.0 20 mm panels Marble and granite are often installed at 20 mm. For exterior panels that is acceptable only when one of these is in place: Edge fixing with proof. The fixing is outside the published geometry rules above, so it is justified by tests of the fixing in the actual stone (ASTM C1354 or EN 13364, wet and dry) and by the engineer's calculation [10] [3] . Expect smaller panels and more fixings. An undercut system. Undercut anchors with a European Technical Assessment are the documented route for hard stone at 20 mm, with stone-specific resistance from the assessment or from tests, four anchors per panel and gauge-checked holes [9] [11] . A thicker panel. Three more points from the published guidance: Epoxy or resin must not carry the load. A flexible connection is needed; rigid epoxy in kerfs has spalled stone through thermal expansion [12] [13] . Mesh on the back of stone is fragment retention and handling protection. We found no published source that lets it count toward panel strength. Marble outdoors can bow and lose strength under repeated heating; in documented cases tests projected a large loss of bending strength [14] . A European test exists for it (EN 16306) [15] . For exterior marble in Riyadh sun, ask the engineer whether it is required. Limestone in undercut systems is a separate case: one maker's data sets 25 to 30 mm minimum for limestone and sandstone, and stone not listed in the assessment needs additional tests [9] . Our typical 30 mm limestone fits that range. Reference drawings Undercut anchors on rails Undercut anchors: back of the panel Typical details for discussion at design stage, not for construction. Notes on these details

6.0 Porcelain The fixing type depends on the slab thickness. In one slab maker's guide, thin slabs of about 3 to 6 mm use adhesive, clips, rivets or frames, while undercut and kerf fixing need the 12 or 20 mm slabs [16] . An undercut anchor assessed for stoneware starts at 8 mm panel thickness, with at least four anchors per panel [17] . ISO/TS 17870-3 covers mechanical fixing of large-format porcelain: fixing systems, wind load factors, anchor pull-out and edge fracture tests, impact and anti-shatter mesh [18] . Wind and impact performance belongs to the tested combination of panel, fixing and substructure, not to the panel alone [16] . Stone habits do not transfer: edge distances and hole depths come from the anchor's assessment. Our undercut experience on porcelain is with 20 mm panels on Hilti undercut anchors.

7.0 Testing Property ASTM EN Why it is asked Absorption and density C97 EN 13755, EN 1936 Classifies the stone [10] [19] Compressive strength C170 EN 1926 Classifies the stone Flexural strength C880 EN 12372 or EN 13161 The value used for panel bending; specimens at project thickness and finish [20] [6] Modulus of rupture C99 Small-prism bending strength used in the material specifications [6] Strength at the fixing C1354 EN 13364 (dowel hole) Measures the breaking load at the fixing in the actual stone; the engineer applies the safety factor [3] Petrography EN 12407 Confirms what the stone is [19] Marble bowing EN 16306 Heat and moisture cycling of marble [15] Anchors to the structure Site pull-out proof tests on the installed wall anchors [21] Reports should be current. US practice as reported asks for data less than three years old; a UK guide accepts older data if the quarry bed has not changed. The project specification decides [20] [22] . Flexural strength is tested wet and dry, and in both directions of the bedding where it matters [20] . "Riyadh limestone" is a trade name covering several quarries and beds. The class and the design strength come from current tests on the actual source, which is why we publish no strength value.

4.0 When it goes wrong Stop Work on the affected area stops when the supervisor, the engineer or the consultant finds something that does not match the approved documents. Record A non-conformance report states what was found, where, and on which panels or anchors. Propose The correction is proposed in writing. Where it changes a material, a fixing or a detail, it goes to the engineer or consultant for approval. Correct and release The correction is carried out, inspected and signed before the area is released.

5.0 Tests and mock-up Anchor pull-out tests On request, pull-out tests on site are arranged with the anchor manufacturer or a testing laboratory, and witnessed by the consultant. The number of tests and the proof load are set by the engineer and the project specification. For reference, published UK practice to BS 8539 tests at least 2.5% of the anchors, and at least three in each area, at 1.5 times the design action; a failure increases the sample [1] . A test report is evidence for the engineer, not an approval in itself [2] . Mock-up On request, a mock-up is built from the approved materials and drawings by the same crew, inspected before the fixings are covered, and kept as the quality benchmark once approved. Guide specifications commonly require one before the work proceeds [3] [4] . Material submittals and samples Submitted for approval: stone samples that show the range, and the data for fixings, brackets and anchors.
6.0 Scope A test or a mock-up is recorded as done only where the project asked for it. The design, the acceptance criteria and the tolerances belong to the project engineer or consultant.

Test reports, where tests were done. The 5-year written workmanship warranty attested by the Chamber of Commerce, issued by the contracting company. 3.0 Inspection The project engineer sets the inspection interval. As general guidance, look at the facade once a year and after any storm or impact, and check for: Cracked, chipped, displaced or loose panels. Joints that have opened, closed or lost their sealant. Rust-coloured or white stains running from a joint. Blocked ventilation openings at the base and top of the cavity. Anything fixed to the facade since handover: signs, lights, cables, cameras. Report anything on this list to the building's engineer and to us before repairing it. A stain or a moved panel is information about what is happening behind the stone.

4.0 Cleaning Remove dust with clean water and a soft brush. Where a cleaner is needed, use a neutral one. Do not use acids or salt-based cleaners on limestone or marble [1] . Test any cleaner on a small hidden area first [2] . Do not use high-pressure washing at close range. Keep irrigation spray and water features off the facade.

5.0 Do not Do not drill into panels or fix anything to them (signs, lights, cables) without engineering approval. Do not fill the ventilation gaps or open joints. Venting the cavity is part of how the facade works [3] . Do not replace a panel with a different stone, thickness or fixing without the engineer's approval. Do not let trades lean ladders or scaffolding on unprotected panel edges.

6.0 Repairs How a panel is replaced depends on the system: Undercut on rails: each panel hangs alone and can be taken off and replaced on its own. Pin, kerf and Up-Down : the fixings sit in the joints and are shared with neighbours, so panels are released in sequence. This is work for the installer. Sealant joints, where the facade has them, have a limited life and are replaced when they crack or lose adhesion. Contact us for any replacement during or after the warranty period. h: Mechanical Fixing vs Wet Cement Fixing
t: Riyadh Heat & Dust How the two methods hold up in Riyadh. Select a row to see why. Mechanical fixing Wet cement fixing Summer heat (45°C) Strong Weak Mechanical fixing Each panel is held by mechanical fixings with a joint around it, so it expands and contracts freely with the daily heat. Wet cement fixing Stone, mortar and wall expand at different rates. Day-and-night heat cycles stress the mortar bond and can open hollow spots behind the stone. Wind & dust storms Strong Fair Mechanical fixing The project engineer calculates the wind load for each project to the current SBC 301 and sets the fixing type and spacing for it. Wet cement fixing Holding power depends on full mortar contact behind every panel, which cannot be checked once the stone is set. Moisture & white stains Strong Weak Mechanical fixing No mortar behind the stone, so no cement salts wash out onto the face: no mortar efflorescence. Wet cement fixing Water moving through cement mortar carries salts to the face and leaves white efflorescence stains, most visible on light Riyadh limestone. Wet cement fixing Replacing a panel means chiselling out mortar, which risks cracking the panels around it. FAQ What stone thickness do you use on mechanically fixed facades? Natural stone is typically 30 mm, thicker on demand. Marble and granite are often 20 mm; exterior 20 mm panels on edge fixings need the engineer's check and stone tests, or an undercut system. Porcelain thickness follows the panel maker's system. How is wind load designed? The project engineer calculates the wind load for each project to the current Saudi Building Code (SBC 301), and that sets the fixing type and spacing. Which fixing systems do you install? Up-Down angle brackets, PEN pin fixing, vertical C-Channel rails, kerf rails and undercut anchors.
